items.article: Fines replace jail terms for first-time ‘false news’ offences under a decree rights groups say is still repressive. Tunisia has softened a cybercrime law that has landed journalists and activists in prison, letting first-time offenders pay fines instead of serving time. The amendment to Decree 54, which went into effect on Wednesday, sets fines of 10,000 to 20,000 Tunisian dinars ($3,370 to $6,740) for a first offence of spreading “false news” and related violations. The fines replace a five-year prison sentence. However, repeat offenders may still face jail. Rights and media freedom advocates in Tunisia and abroad have long opposed the decree as repressive, saying it has been wielded against President Kais Saied’s opposition, activists and reporters. The government, meanwhile, says the decree protects people and public order from attack, and is needed to tackle online crime and disinformation. So what has changed, how has the decree been used, and why has Tunisia softened it now?

items.text: I've visited UK's second best seaside town - I won't be going back again
items.article: The seaside town has a lot of fans, but I'm not one of them It's rare to head to the Scottish Highlands and leave feeling underwhelmed. Across my 34 years, I've clocked up well over a year in Scotland's western mountains, and like everyone, I've fallen for plenty of the region's corners. There's the impossibly tranquil and beautiful village of Glenelg, tucked away from the world's pressures on the far side of the Mam Ratagan Pass. Follow the coast a little further and you'll reach Sandaig, a shore of pure white sand with scallops bubbling in the shallows, which inspired Gavin Maxwell to write 'Ring of Bright Water'. If you only have an afternoon and want to soak up as much Highland scenery as you can, it's hard to beat a trip on the West Highlands Line. This railway, once named the world's most beautiful, carries you over moorland, around lochs and through mountain passes, and only Switzerland can really compete. items.article: One of the 7 Cornell frat brothers accused of gang raping a fellow student allegedly called a sorority member to instruct a friend of hers not to discuss what she "thinks" may have happened on the night in question. The sorority member -- who was at Chi Phi the night of the alleged gang rape -- told investigators one of the accused rang her up the next day to make sure a friend of hers didn't "say anything that she thinks might've happened last night" ... CBS News reports. She ended up passing the message along, and her friend told investigators that the message "clicked" when Cornell sent an alert email about the sexual assault. That friend told investigators ... "It makes a lot more sense ... And it was very concerning." She and her roommate eventually talked to the Cornell University Police Department ... but she told investigators that she didn't know what came of her statement. As for the accused ... he first denied ever making that phone call in his chat with investigators before changing his tune in a written correction a month later ... saying that the conversation's topic was about "not spreading any rumors." He also said in his initial interview that the frat's game plan about the rumors was "just deny."
